utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-10/1-S, the Prosecutor versus Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Cesic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Judge El Mahdi, Judge Liu, Mr. Bakrac. My name is Mark Harmon. I'm a senior prosecutor for the Office of the Prosecutor. To my right is Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky; to my left is Mr. Tom Hannis who will elocute for the Prosecutor in this afternoon's proceedings; and to his left is Susan Grogan, who is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and my learned colleagues from the Prosecution, my name is Mihajlo Bakrac, and I represent the accused, Mr. Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bakrac. We're here in a sentencing hearing, as a consequence of a guilty plea that has been entered by you, Mr. Cesic, on the 8th of October of this year in which you have pleaded guilty to 12 counts, and if I may just summarise it very, very briefly, that was on five cases of murder, sometimes multiple murder, and one case of sexual abuse. That's the basis on which we work. I was informed that there is an issue as far as the facts are concerned, and if any of the parties would like to address the Chamber in that respect, please do so. Mr. Tochilovsky. I'm using the wrong name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Tom Hannis from the Office of the Prosecutor. I would like to address that, thank you. Actually, there is one of about three housekeeping matters I would like to address before we go into the substance of this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence aware of all the housekeeping matters? Are they informed about what to expect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One they're not but I believe it is no surprise and no significance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would please indicate which one so that we --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first matter I want to address regards the name of the victim in counts 5 and 6. The indictment names the victim as Mirsad Glavovic. Since the change of plea and in the course of contacting victims about victim impact, we received information from the Bosnian authorities that this victim's true name is Mirsad Mujagic, M-U-J-A-G-I-C with a half banana. We've informed Mr. Bakrac of that. I believe he's discussed it with his client, and we are all satisfied that, as far as the individual who was killed in that incident, we are talking about the same person. We got the name Glavovic from one of the witness statements that there were, I believe, three witnesses who talked about that particular incident in which Mirsad, who was a Muslim policeman in Brcko, was singled out by Mr. Cesic, was forced to go around and shake hands and say farewell to all the other detainees before he was taken outside, beaten and shot. The other two witnesses who speak of this incident only knew the victim by his first name Mirsad or a nickname Mirso, but all knew him as a policeman. So based on all the information we have and from discussion with defence counsel, who has consulted with his client, we believe we are talking about the same person. We would propose to amend the indictment to show this additional name or true name of Mujagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's your procedural suggestion for solving that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could briefly mention the other issues so that we know what in what order to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The other matter is one that Defence counsel had not been advised of, but on page 2, paragraph 8 of our initial sentencing brief filed on 12 November, the procedural background indicates that the guilty plea was entered on 8 September 2002. That is an error. That should read 8 October 2003. And we would move to make that correction at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that, Mr. Bakrac, there is no objection to this amendment of the sentencing brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any objections to make, but if I could take this opportunity to comment on the first issue. I can confirm everything's been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at issue, and then we know this -- but this was such a futile one, of course -- minor one that I thought it wise to deal with it right away. So it's on the record that your brief is corrected, it's now 8th of October, 2003, the date on which the accused entered his guilty plea. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to return to the name of the victim. I should also indicate that if we are going to correct his name or add his true name, Mujagic, that change should be made in the plea agreement in the factual basis as well as in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was your third point or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could have your third point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The third point was merely to confirm, Mr. President, with you, and Your Honours, if you have received all four filings we have made regarding sentencing. The first was our sentencing brief filed on 12 November. The second was the unredacted statement of detainee, the victim in count 7 and 8. The third was our supplemental information relating to sentencing filed on the 21st, and the fourth was filed just yesterday, that's further supplemental information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's of the 26th. It was filed where you analyse some of the material you received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was 51 -- that included 51 pages of B/C/S documents for which we do not yet have an English translation but relate to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You indicated that you would immediately present it to the Defence as well. I take it Mr. Bakrac that you at least have received it. I'm not asking any further comment at the moment but you are in possession of copies of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have received a copy of those documents. I was informed about this, and I found it in my locker, and it's my intention and the intention of my client to assist the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution in establishing the truth, and to this end I have attempted to review those documents, and in my closing argument, I will comment on the documents that I received yesterday. Naturally I have received all the previous documents my learned colleague has mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That goes into the substance of the matter, so perhaps we first now return to the issue of the family name of the victim of counts 5 and 6. Mr. Bakrac, do you have any suggestion as to the procedural way of dealing with that issue? Do you join Mr. Hannis in amending the indictment, that this would be the proper way to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for asking me about this matter. There is really nothing in particular I would like to request, but since you have allowed me to address you and to express my opinion, I think that -- I think that in the transcript of this case and later on we could indicate that in that part of the indictment, the factual basis is being amended so as to avoid a procedure which would involve amending the indictment and the factual basis. This is my suggestion, but I think that it might be simpler if the transcript, which is regarded as valid, were used as a basis for the decision of the Trial Chamber, and I think that this would be one way of correcting this error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You suggest a more -- I would say a more simpler, more practical approach. Yes, Mr. Hannis. Since we had been informed about this issue perhaps to be raised today, the Chamber has already given it some thought and also noticed that if you change the indictment, then of course a lot of other things have to be changed as well, that means plea agreement, plea, conviction pronounced. So that would be -- so before we would invite you to follow that course and apart from the question whether from a procedural point of view amending an indictment after a conviction has been pronounced on it might be an acrobatic exercise from a procedural point of view. So before I invite you, I would rather try to seek whether the parties could follow the Chamber in the following approach: One of the issues at stake, I would say, is whether the -- whether there's a possibility that the plea has been equivocal. Perhaps we first try to investigate that a bit more in detail. And I would like to ask Defence already to prepare that if later on a question would be put to the accused whether he would have entered any -- whether he would have concluded any other plea agreement or whether he would have entered any other plea as he did if he would have known at that time that the name was different, that's -- the Defence is prepared to answer that question. I -- let's first concentrate on what Mr. Cesic exactly pleaded guilty to on the 8th of October of this year. The transcript literally reads, after I had invited Madam Registrar to read count 5 and after count 5 was read as follows: "Count 5, a violation of the laws or customs of wars recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) murder, of the Geneva Conventions. I then asked Mr. Cesic, how do you plead, Mr. Cesic? And the accused, according to the interpreted answer was, "Guilty, Your Honour." I then said the Trial Record records the plea of guilty on count 5 and I invited Madam Registrar to read count 6 which read as follows: Count 6, a violations of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 5(a), murder, of the Tribunal Statute. I then invited Mr. Cesic to enter a plea. I asked him, "Do you plead guilty or not guilty" and Mr. Cesic according to the transcript in English said, "Guilty, Your Honour." So that's exactly the words he used in court when he pleaded guilty. As far as the conviction is concerned, the transcript says, and that's on page 92, line 17, my words were the following: "Mr. Cesic, the Chamber accepts your guilty plea on all 12 counts of the indictment brought against you as amended in November 2002, and this Chamber finds you guilty on each of the 12 counts as they have been read to you prior to entering your guilty plea." The Chamber takes it that the plea agreement concluded between the Prosecution and the Defence and the accused was the very basis which made the accused to enter a guilty plea. Attached to that agreement was the factual basis on which the agreement was concluded. And also that factual basis has been read out in Court, and the relevant part reads as follows: "In respect of counts 5 and 6, on or about the 11th of May, 1992 --" that's how I read it to the accused on the 8th of October -- "you called the Muslim policeman Mirsad Glavovic from the main hangar building at Luka camp where Glavovic was being detained. You ordered Mr. Glavovic to say good-bye and shake hands with the other detainees, and then, Mr. Cesic, you took Mirsad Glavovic outside the hangar building where he and others -- where you and others beat and killed the victim. You also agree that you intended to kill Mirsad Glavovic at the time of the beating I just described." That's on page 64 and 65 of the transcript of the 8th of October. As it now turns out, the parties have discovered that the -- that one element of the factual basis relates to counts 5 and 6 is in need of correction. The name of the victim was not Mirsad Glavovic but Mirsad Mujagic. The Trial Chamber does understand that the accused - but I'll verify that - knew the first name of the victim, who was a police officer, to be Mirsad, but was unaware of his family name, and I would like to verify this in order to better understand whether this was a mistake. So therefore, first, Mr. Cesic, I would like to ask you, when you signed the plea agreement, were you aware of both the first and the family name of the victim of this beating up and finally killing this person, or were you aware of both his first name and his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only knew the victim's first name, but that was the person concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you not have concluded the plea agreement if you would have known that the family name of this victim was different from the name we find, the family name we find in the attachment to the plea agreement? If you want to consult with counsel, of course you could do so. So would you have not concluded the plea agreement if you would have known that the family name was Mujagic rather than Glavovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I knew who the person concerned was, all they did was omit this surname, but I would have signed it because I knew who this person was. So this person was called Mirso, his nickname was Mirso.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would have concluded, under the same conditions, the plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you, if you would have known the difference in family name, would you have entered any other plea than you did on the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I didn't know the person's family name but I did know who the person concerned was, that's why I stated what I did. But if that had been different, I think that we would have solved this issue in discussions with the Prosecution and my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it would not have caused you to enter a plea of not guilty on counts 5 and 6? If you want to consult with counsel, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have entered the same plea of guilty on that count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cesic. I do take it that there are no other corrections necessary to the factual basis apart from the one we discussed at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, you don't protest, so I take it that you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the correction the factual basis is in need of makes, as we just heard from the Defence and from the accused - I should say the convicted person - makes the plea not any less informed or unequivocal than it was before. The family name of the victim alone has no bearing, no specific bearing on the actus reus or the mens rea of this crime other, of course, than exclusively the detail of the civil identity of the victim, which is not a material element in the Prosecutor's case. Whether the policeman detained and killed was Mirsad A, B or Mirsad C is not a material element. Therefore, the guilty plea which does not actually name the victim stands unaffected, and the conviction which does not also directly mention the name of the victim is also unaffected. What needs a slight correction, therefore, is the factual basis on which the plea agreement and the guilty plea rest. Nevertheless, it is important for the family of the victim and also for the relevance of statements presented by the Prosecution to establish that the underlying factual basis on which the plea was based was not in every detail correct, and the Chamber now understands that the factual basis on which the parties agreed is limited to the first name of the witness being Mirsad and that the family name is struck from the factual basis on which the parties concluded their agreement on which the plea was entered and on which the finding, which of course had this effect, although not in words, on the decision of the Trial Chamber. The Chamber considers the matter sufficiently solved in this way. Having dealt with this matter, I think I could give an opportunity for the Prosecution to submit whatever it wants to submit at this moment in regard to sentencing to the Chamber. That, as far as I understand, it's then the intention of Mr. Cesic to make an unsworn statement, and then finally, you, Mr. Bakrac, will make your submissions to the Chamber. And whenever there would be any questions remaining, the Chamber will put them at the end of your submissions. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As you indicated before, Mr. Cesic has been convicted now of five separate counts of murder as violations of the laws and customs of war, and five counts of murder as crimes against humanity, both referring to five separate incidents; and also to a sexual assault charge, both as a crime against humanity and a violation of the law and customs of war. These five separate incidents involve the murder of ten different human beings, and the sexual assault involves an offence against two individuals. The task before Your Honours at this point is not an easy one. Any time we're faced with deciding what is an appropriate punishment when a single human life has been lost is a difficult one. You can see in the statements from the relatives of some of the murder victims that their view is that these crimes that occurred should bring the accused - in one case I think the victim recommended 30 years, and in all the others, they felt he deserved a life sentence. Our Statute, in Article 24, sets out the factors for you to consider in arriving at an appropriate sentence. Gravity of the offence has been described as the primary consideration. In addition, you need to consider the individual circumstances of the accused. In addition to Article 24, our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, at Rule 101, provide that the Court should also take into account aggravating circumstances, mitigating circumstances including cooperation, and the general sentencing practices in the former Yugoslavia. Your Honour, with regard to the gravity of the offence, as we indicated in our brief, these crimes were shocking and senseless in their cruelty, and we believe they were of the utmost gravity. They forever ended the lives of the ten victims and they forever changed for the worse the lives of those two brothers who were the victims of the sexual assault and the lives of the relatives -- the surviving relatives of the murder victims. The impact on the living victims, both the direct and indirect victims, is detailed in attachments A through D to our brief that was filed on 12 November. With regard to aggravating circumstances, Your Honour, I just want to refer to a few that we believe exist in this case and are mentioned in our brief. With regard to the sexual assault charges in counts 7 and 8, we believe the Celebici case, where it talks about public rape as being an act of unusual depravity, would apply to the situation in which these two brothers were forced to commit an act of oral sodomy upon one another in the presence of other guards in addition to Mr. Cesic. As for all the counts, we believe that the Aleksovski case, at paragraph 227, stands for the proposition that crimes of this nature inflicted upon vulnerable victims are an aggravating circumstance that the Court can consider in imposing sentence. All the victims in these counts were vulnerable in the sense that they were detained and at the mercy of Mr. Cesic and the other guards at the Luka camp in Brcko. The Furundzija case, in paragraph 283, indicates that when the victims are civilians that also may be considered an aggravating factor. Once more with regard to the sexual assault counts, we would indicate that the humiliating nature of that offence was of unusual depravity, as discussed in Celebici, and is further grounds to treat that as an aggravating factor. Two others that I would like to bring to your attention, Your Honour, relate to the -- the multiple murders in this case. We have five separate counts that involve the killing of ten individuals, occurred on five different occasions over at least a ten-day or two-week period, if not longer. This was not an event in which ten individuals were killed on one occasion as an act of revenge because a comrade has been killed in battle or because a relative has been killed in the war, but these were five separate occasions. Mr. Cesic had the opportunity between times to reflect upon what he had done when he had killed another individual. I have no case that supports this exact proposition, Your Honour, but we would suggest it to you as something that you might possibly consider in the circumstances of this case. Each time, after the first murder of the five victims and before he killed the fisherman who was mentioned in counts 3 and 4, he had time to reflect about what he had done. Likewise between that murder and the subsequent murders. Finally, Your Honour, we would argue that one additional aggravating factor has to do with abuse of authority. Mr. Cesic was a member of the Territorial Defence in early May 1992, and on about the 15th of May, 1992, according to his military book, he became a member of the reserve policemen, although the circumstances indicate that he seemed to be acting as a policeman earlier than that. He was at Luka camp, and as indicated in the Defence sentencing memo in paragraphs 51 to 53, he apparently had some authority because he was able to assist some individuals who had been detained at Luka camp in that he was able to get them released and able to help them get their identity cards returned to them. We believe this shows that he did have some authority, although he was about no means a high-ranking official or a high-level policeman or soldier. With regard to mitigating circumstances, we agree, Your Honour, that the following mitigating circumstances do exist in this case: First of all, Mr. Cesic did plead guilty, and he pled guilty early in this case, before the pre-trial briefs were required to be filed, and the case law indicates that that is a mitigating circumstance that the Court should take into consideration. In addition, his guilty plea assists in the mission of this Tribunal to establish truth and try to bring about reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia. Also, Your Honours, as we indicated in our plea agreement, Mr. Cesic has cooperated, and we believe that is an additional grounds for mitigation. Finally, Your Honour, I want to address some of the points that were raised in the defendant's sentencing brief. These are points that we disagree with learned counsel, Mr. Bakrac. In paragraphs 33, 40, 41, and in paragraph 49, the Defence speaks about the charged offences of which he is convicted as being isolated incidents and talks about his good character before the incidents and after the incidents. We have no dispute with the evidence that he's submitted in his brief that Mr. Cesic apparently did help certain non-Serbs in Brcko, those who lived in his building or in his neighbourhood, those that by witness accounts he helped get released from Luka camp. But we believe on balance of the probabilities that that doesn't outweigh other evidence of character that was contrary to his claim of no bad acts before or after the two-week period in May 1992. And I will address that further in a moment. With regard to the abuse of trust, Defence counsel argues that this should not apply. As I mentioned earlier, we believe that his apparent or actual authority to assist prisoners at Luka camp indicates that he was in a position of some trust and obviously we believe his killings and forced sexual assault was an abuse of that trust. In paragraph 39, the defendant makes a reference to the fact that most of these individuals who were killed were instantly killed. Your Honour, we can't imagine imagination any circumstances in which that should be treated as mitigation. In counts 1 and 2, the first incident, five men were killed at one time and the mechanics of operating a gun and shooting people would indicate that they weren't all killed instantly at the same time. Some would have had time to anticipate their own death once the shooting began. With regard to Mirsad the policeman in counts 5 and 6, the factual basis indicates that he was beaten and shot. He was also required to go around and shake the hands ever all the detainees in the hangar before he was taken out and killed. He had time to anticipate his death before it occurred, and it was not an instant killing. And likewise the victim in counts 9 and 10 was beaten by Mr. Cesic and that was not an instant killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask, you Mr. Hannis, to look at the transcript on page 16. You see there is a part missing between 3, 40, 01 and 21. Could you please repeat what you said there in order to have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe that's where I was indicating that in paragraphs 39 of the Defence pre-trial brief, they make reference to the fact that most of the victims of the murders were instantly killed and it's our position that that is not something that should be considered as a mitigating factor. Thank you for pointing that out, Your Honour. The last thing I want to return to the issue of good character evidence. In our submissions, our last submission and our next to the last submission, we provide the Court with some evidence indicating, first of all, there was some reputation evidence about Mr. Cesic's statements from four different witnesses to the effect that they had known Mr. Cesic before the war and believed that he had been engaged in criminal activity or in trouble with the police. That was not offered as an aggravating circumstance but only to deal with the Defence position that he was of good character before the war and after the offences charged. And our last submission filed yesterday which contains I believe about 51 pages of documents from the Brcko basic court, the Brcko military court, the supreme military court and the Brcko police station relate to two separate incidents. One was in December of 1991, before the war, in which Mr. Cesic was charged with another individual for a count of assault resulting in serious bodily injury. That case by -- the document apparently has not been resolved. The investigation proceeded to a point in time when the Prosecutor recommended it be suspended because the defendants, Mr. Cesic and another Muslim individual could not be located and it was recommended that prosecution be suspended until that obstacle could be removed. With regard to the second matter, Mr. Cesic, by the documents we received was convicted of what I understand the translation to be negligent homicide. The murder of a friend of his in February of 1993. He was tried in the military court. He appealed his conviction. That was upheld on appeal and he was sentenced to three years in prison less credit for time served in which it appears he had done ten months in pre-trial detention. He didn't immediately appear for his sentence but was arrested, I believe, in August of 1996 according to the documents we received. And again, Your Honour, not offered as an aggravating circumstance because we don't believe that's proper under the law. But to rebut the argument that these were isolated incidents, and to rebut the argument of good character. One additional factor in -- mentioned in the Defence pre-trial brief as a mitigating factor is remorse. At this point in time we can't take any position, Your Honour, because we haven't heard his expression of remorse. He has pled guilty, but we contend that that is not the same as an expression of remorse. There needs to be something apart and separate, above and beyond the mere acceptance of responsibility. Lastly in the defendant's pre-trial brief, Your Honour, my learned colleague lists several cases, pointing out sentences that have been imposed in other cases in this Tribunal. I'm not going to go through them one by one, but we would urge Your Honours that upon a close examination of the facts in each of those cases, you will find that they can all be distinguished or differentiated from the facts of this case and the individual circumstances of this accused. All things considered, Your Honour, we believe that the gravity of this -- of these offences and the aggravating circumstances we have pointed to in our sentencing brief versus the defendant's cooperation and any other mitigating circumstances you feel may have been proved by the Defence, considered together show that an appropriate sentence in this case would be within the range of 13 to 18 years, as we have agreed to in our plea agreement and recommended to the Court. If there are no questions for me at this time, I will sit down and await Defence counsel's argument. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. The Chamber has no questions for you at this very moment. Mr. Bakrac, I do understand that Mr. Cesic would like to make a statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, this is correct. And I ask you to give him leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cesic, you have an opportunity to make a statement, if you want.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, without any false sentiments, I wish to express my deep remorse for all the evil I have done. Words such as "remorse" are insufficient to express what somebody like me feels. Looking back in time after so much time has elapsed since I committed those crimes, there is an enormous difference between my state of mind now and then. Now I would never do the things I did then, the things that took place in a time of euphoria, a time when all human dignity was abolished. Before the trial, I pleaded guilty to the counts of the indictment, and I did my best to help the Office of the Prosecutor and the Tribunal to bring to light a small part of the overall truth, the part that refers to my actions. Your Honours, I will do anything to bring back the past and not to do what I have done. Since this is not possible, all that is left for me is to feel the deepest remorse for what I have done. To this I would like to add that I did not want to bring my friends and relatives here to say nice things about me because I didn't want to increase the pain of the victims and their families, out of respect for the deceased. I hope that my sincere remorse, which I feel deeply, will help to prevent similar things from happening in the future, and I wish to say that any people that experiences war is unfortunate, and people who live through this and families who have suffered pain feel this deeply. I want to say that I hope nobody will ever do the things that I have done and that prison is not the only punishment for me, because it is even harder to go on living with this feeling of guilt. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving me leave to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cesic. Mr. Bakrac, I'm looking at the clock. How much time do you think you would need for your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not very good at estimating the time I will take, but I think about 45 minutes would be sufficient. I do apologise if I overstep that limit, but I think I won't need more than 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we perhaps could finish before our first break. Until the first break, that would be approximately 40 minutes. If it would be possible for you to use some 40 minutes, which is close to what you indicated you would need, and if you would perhaps look at the clock now and then when proceeding so you can keep track of whether you lose or whether you gain speed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, in its sentencing brief which it submitted on the 12th of October, as stated, the Defence mentioned all the aspects that we feel should be taken into consideration when sentencing the accused. The Defence gave a brief introduction stating the background of this case as well as its view of the law to be applied. Therefore, we feel it would be superfluous to repeat orally all that has been stated in the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite clear, the Chamber has read all the written submissions, so you -- there is no need to repeat any of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is precisely what I wish to say, so that I will pass over the introduction and the applicable law, and I will refer to the essence of the issue that has brought us all here, and that is determining a just sentence for the accused Cesic, taking into consideration all the circumstances that have been established. The Defence can agree with the Prosecution in the following: The fundamental issue to be considered in sentencing in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is the gravity of the offence. Wishing to analyse the criminal offence as fully as possible and as professionally as possible, I realise that the Defence might bring pain to the victims of sexual abuse and to the families of the deceased, and for this reason I apologise in advance to the families of the victims and to the victims if what I will now say increases their pain or gives them further -- causes them further suffering. However, when considering the gravity of the offence, we cannot avoid -- avoid inflicting pain perhaps on the families of the victims and the victims and hurting their feelings. What we wish to say about the gravity of the offence is that the Defence agrees that murder is one of the most serious crimes. However, in any system of law, there are degrees. There is murder, there is aggravated murder, so that this honourable motivation can aggravate a murder. The criminal offence of murder in itself is a very grave offence. If we look at five incidents, the five incidents of which Cesic has been found guilty, we shall see that in three of those incidents this was a momentary murder that was committed by firing shots from a firearm. In two cases, the murders were a result of beatings. In most of these murders, the murder did not lead to additional suffering on the part of the victims. Of course murder in itself implies suffering, both of the victim and their families. This suffering is subsumed in the elements of murder as such. If we know that there are cases of murder where certain persons are tortured additionally, subjected to additional suffering, then murder which leads to instantaneous death is on the lowest rung of the ladder, so to speak, where murder is concerned. In only two cases were there beatings of the murder victims, and the accused participated in these beatings as part of a group. So it is difficult to establish his dominant role. Therefore, in these five counts of the indictment relating to the crime of murder, one must bear in mind the fact that the victims were not subjected to additional torture and additional suffering apart from the suffering that is implied in the nature of murder itself. With respect to another crime with which the accused is charged and which differs from murder is sexual assault. I think that only one sentence from a statement by only one of the persons who were victims of this should be read out. I am convinced that the Prosecution did not overlook this sentence intentionally, but I feel it can reflect the gravity of the crime that should be taken into consideration in sentencing. In the statement of a witness made on the 7th of November, 2003, that is directly before the trial was to begin and when the guilty plea was already imminent, one of the victims of sexual abuse, person A, says he could not believe that a person like Ranko Cesic would be able to do something like this. He says that he and his brother were respectable people, that he knew Ranko Cesic from before, and that he believes that persons superior to Ranko Cesic instructed him or ordered him to do what he did. If on the 7th of November, 2003, when Ranko Cesic had already been brought before the Tribunal, one of the direct victims of sexual mistreatment says that he cannot believe that a person like Ranko could do something like this and that he feels that he must have received orders from a superior. This is relevant to the gravity of the offence which the Defence agrees is a very serious offence, and if the motive is to humiliate the victim, then certainly it is a very serious time. With regard to the gravity of crimes, although the Defence is aware of the facts, the jurisprudence, and in other cases before this Tribunal it's been determined that in comparison to -- comparing the case to other cases has or may have limited value. Nevertheless, the Defence has to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that in a certain sense, making comparisons could be useful, especially when trying to determine the gravity of the offences with which Mr. Cesic has been charged. Similarly, the jurisprudence in previous decisions in this Tribunal is consistent and has been determined that the crime of persecution is one of the most serious crimes, and it is a sort of umbrella crime which covers other crimes, and criminal acts, especially murder and sexual abuse, et cetera, which have been committed as persecution, are to be treated as far more serious times. What determines the gravity of the crimes committed by Ranko Cesic with regard to the majority of the decisions of this Tribunal is that these crimes don't fall under the heading of persecution. They don't belong to that category. So the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, that is to say making comparisons to other cases, could be of use. This is why the Defence also considers, and we will address the Prosecution's brief and other documents that the Prosecution has submitted, we will comment on these later. We believe that the acts are isolated incidents which took place within a five- or ten-day period, but everything else, and we will analyse this later, has no connection to these crimes with which the accused has been charged and for which he has declared guilty. The matter of the position of the accused when he committed these crimes is also a significant matter when determining the gravity of the crimes. My learned colleague, the Prosecutor, did not dispute the fact that Mr. Cesic, the accused, was first of all a member of the Territorial Defence from the 1st to the 15th of May and then a member of the reserve police force from the 15th of May to the 20th of June, and then a member of the military district. And the Defence has also submitted to the Trial Chamber evidence in addition to its brief. It is clear to this Trial Chamber on the basis of the jurisprudence to date that all those who participated in war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all these people were members of the Territorial Defence. Likewise, it's not in dispute that Mr. Cesic was a member of the reserve police force, but he didn't have a rank of any kind. After the 22nd of June, Ranko Cesic was an ordinary soldier when the army and the military district were established, and you can see that from his military booklet. He was a soldier who didn't have a rank of any kind. And when we make comparisons with certain other cases such as the Todorovic case and other cases that have appeared before the Tribunal, we will see that apart from the fact that Mr. Cesic hasn't been accused for these crimes under the heading of persecution, this diminishes the gravity of the crime. Similarly, he is not a person who was in a position of any particular importance. I respect my colleagues from the Prosecution. I appreciate all the cooperation we have had that has enabled us to reach an agreement on this case, but I have to say that using an official position in a certain way, well there is nothing to back this up, abusing a position in a certain way is not backed up. He didn't have the position of a superior. He had no authority. It is quite clear that there is no evidence to back this up. On the contrary, there is evidence provided by the Defence that proves the contrary. If we bear in mind another fact which is not in dispute, and that is that the Defence, with regard to determining the sentence, must establish beyond reasonable doubt -- must establish its case beyond reasonable doubt, then the Prosecution's position that Cesic did have authority and did abuse his position is not a correct position, and this is not something that can be considered by the Trial Chamber. On the contrary, the Defence has provided evidence, and it's contained in the military booklet of the accused, evidence that shows where Ranko Cesic served and evidence that shows that he didn't hold a rank of any kind. He didn't have the position of a superior. If we bear all these factors, all these elements in mind, then this crime cannot be qualified as having this seriousness, and the participation of the accused was very low-level participation. In addition to what we have said, this is one of the rare cases in which the accused has been charged with crimes that don't fall under the heading of persecution. And in comparison to the Todorovic case, for example, we can say that the accused didn't have any command responsibility, he didn't hold the position of a superior, he didn't hold a position that he could have abused and which would entail treating his crime as a more serious crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Bakrac. Many of the things you're telling us appear in almost similar wordings in your sentencing brief as well, whereas on other issues you seem not to respond to what really seems to be the issue raised by the Prosecution. For example, you have now explained to us that Mr. Cesic had certainly no formal authority. I think that is also the position of the Prosecution. So therefore, it's no need. I think the parties agree on that. But the issue raised by the Prosecution was that on the basis of the material submitted by the Defence itself, and I think they might have specially referred to paragraph 53 in which we find an excerpt of something that happened in a camp, in the Luka camp, where, for example, it reads that person stating that "when he saw me, he nodded and asked me to go with him. He ordered to one of the soldiers to find my identity card and to give me a pass which -- which I could go around." I think that's the issue raised. You do not disagree on the formal position of Mr. Cesic. The Prosecution seems to accept that but points at the fact that in your own material words appear like "ordering other soldiers" and "taking people out of a camp." I think that's the issue, and instead of repeating -- of course you can refer briefly to what you have put in your pre-sentencing brief, but that's really one of the issues, I think, that the Chamber needs assistance to decide on that issue which seems to be -- at least, that's how I understand the Prosecution argument, there seems to be some contradiction, to say on the one hand there was no position whatsoever, he was the lowest of the lowest, he had no authority whatsoever, and at the same time the material says that he ordered something or that he did a few things which at least suggest some authority or some power. I think these are the issues the Chamber really needs your comment on rather than to hear -- although I will not prevent you from briefly indicating what the position of Defence is, but on hearing again what is already set out in quite some detail in the sentencing brief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, naturally it was my intention to address that issue and that was the matter I was just going to address. In my brief I didn't state that he issued an order. That is contained in one of the witness's statements where it is stated that Ranko Cesic helped -- helped them. That's their impression. And at that time, the possibility of helping someone, getting someone out of a camp does not by itself mean anything. You may not have an official position, but this doesn't mean you have a de facto position. It might be a matter of taking advantage of an opportunity. Perhaps someone doesn't know who is in charge. Perhaps it is a matter of using acquaintances from before the war. The possibility of helping someone at a given moment in time by itself does not allow one to assume that the person in question had de facto authority, and this is why I believe that one should bear in mind the fact that the accused did not have any authority in the economic, political, or military sense. What one could assume, and it would be logical to come to this conclusion, is that at a given moment perhaps some people were there who would raise no objections and it might be possible to help someone get out of a camp. The word "ordered" is something that was stated by a witness, a word used by a witness, and I don't think that this means that the accused was in a position of authority. I don't want to repeat myself, I don't want to repeat everything that's been stated in the sentencing brief, but I will just turn to another matter very briefly which is not contained in the sentencing brief. I will just turn to certain considerations of the Prosecution with regard to aggravating circumstances. The Defence, in its sentencing brief, has already stated that in the Defence opinion there are no particular aggravating circumstances, because everything that could be taken into consideration as aggravating circumstances is already incorporated in the gravity of the crime. It already forms part of the gravity of the crime and that is why it is still my position that there are no aggravating circumstances with respect to the accused. But I would also like to turn to the matter that the Prosecution addressed in its sentencing brief with regard to aggravating circumstances. One of the items is that we should take the fact that the victims were vulnerable, helpless, and inferior citizens -- citizens in an inferior position as an aggravating circumstance. And the Defence can very briefly respond to this by saying that these facts are incorporated in the gravity of the crime and cannot subsequently be added to the crime and considered to be -- considered as aggravating circumstances. I think that the jurisprudence with regard to this matter is such that a crime against humanity incorporates this. A crime against humanity - and Mr. Cesic has pleaded guilty to this - includes the fact that it affects civilians, vulnerable and helpless civilians. To take this fact into consideration as an aggravating circumstance, in my opinion, would be contrary to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and contrary to a certain concept of international justice. In the Banovic sentence in paragraph 50, I think the position expressed is identical to the one that I have just put forward. The Prosecution in its brief also stated that it is necessary to determine what the accused did with regard to detainees A and B and this should be taken into consideration as an aggravating circumstance. With regard to what they were forced to do, I think that this form of humiliation with regard to determining the gravity of that crime, I think that this is incorporated in the crime itself, and I'd like to repeat everything we've been able to see from one of the witness's statement. I would like to emphasise what was stated in that statement. So these arguments that the Prosecution has put forward with regard to the aggravating circumstances are not correct because a crime against humanity with which Mr. Cesic has been charged includes a systematic attack against -- assumes that there was a systematic attack against a civilian population, so therefore is incorporated in the act. When we're talking about mitigating circumstances, I don't want to repeat what is already set forth in the brief, but I must emphasise the fact that a guilty plea at a very early stage, if the accused pleads guilty, which he did at a very early stage, this is significant and we compare it to the Todorovic case where the Trial Chamber found that his guilty plea should be given its full significance because it was entered 26 months after his initial appearance. If that's the case, we must emphasise that Mr. Cesic entered a guilty plea 16 months after his initial appearance, and as the second Defence counsel for Mr. Cesic, I was aware of the fact that the accused was prepared to enter a guilty plea from the very beginning. I now have to turn to a matter that has been the subject of consideration on the part of the Tribunal's jurisprudence with regard to entering a guilty plea. Full and substantial cooperation and a guilty plea have to be taken into consideration as mitigating circumstances. This has been the case in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. I must emphasise, and this is something that was mentioned by the Prosecution in its brief, I must emphasise that Mr. Cesic has fully cooperated with the Prosecution. It has been -- his cooperation has been substantial and sincere. In certain cases it has been stated that entering a guilty plea or cooperating with the Prosecution is something that occurs because it is to the benefit of the accused in the case of substantial cooperation with the Prosecution, and the Rules of the Tribunal provide for this possibility. It's been established that substantial cooperation with the Prosecution shall be taken to constitute mitigating circumstances. But we can't then be -- enter a contradiction and say -- we can't contradict ourselves and say that the accused thought he would benefit from this. In the Todorovic case, the Trial Chamber found that such cooperation had to be taken to be sincere and that the procedure itself allows for the possibility of cooperation, and it has to be to the benefit of the accused. In such situations when the accused tells his Defence counsel that he wants to enter a guilty plea in order to show his remorse, then it is the duty of professional lawyers - we are all aware of this fact - that when discussing with the opposing side, this should be beneficial to the accused. As a result, one cannot then claim that the accused wanted to benefit from such a plea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is there any disagreement between Prosecution and Defence on these issues that you're discussing at this moment? I do understand that you say that a guilty plea and you're also, I think, referring to remorse, but at least cooperation with the Prosecution should be mitigating. Is there any disagreement on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please proceed. And would you please concentrate on issues that are in dispute rather than those on which there seems to be a perfect agreement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to explain the reason for which I have stated these things. I am convinced that the accused's remorse is absolutely sincere. I know this is the case, but naturally this is something that the Trial Chamber has to determine. I just wanted to demonstrate that apart from simply declaring that the accused felt remorse, the fact that the accused pleaded guilty on all counts in the indictment supports the claim that his remorse is sincere. So the reason for which I wanted to state my position with regard to these two matters is that I wanted to provide the Trial Chamber with additional information to convince the Trial Chamber that the remorse felt by the accused for what he did is quite sincere. And to try and conclude, I would just like to turn to matters of disagreement between the Prosecution and the Defence. We disagree with regard to the accused's good character. You and the Defence, we have received certain documents to back up these claims. I don't have to remind the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution that it is the Prosecution's duty to establish certain facts beyond reasonable doubt, to prove certain facts beyond reasonable doubt, and the facts that are the basis for the sentence and which could also be the basis upon -- which could also be the basis for aggravating circumstances. If we have such a situation, then certain facts that have not been proved can't be taken to be arguments, refute the other party's position. If the Prosecution has submitted certain documents and this has not been proved, certain documents in order to back up the statements made by the Defence on the good character of the accused, well, then in such a case we would give these documents the necessary weight. Such documents can't have any weight as evidence. What can be taken to be aggravating circumstances can only be contained in the factual basis, in facts that are not in dispute. In the additional material provided by the Prosecution you have two statements made by two witnesses about alleged cases of rape or attempts to rape. If these facts had been proved, they would be contained in the indictment. These facts can't be taken into consideration even if it's only to refute the Defence's argument that the accused has a good character. This has not been proved. These allegations have not been proved, so they can't be taken into consideration. If we also have a look at the two statements, you will see that in both statements the accused is described in a totally different way, in a way that does not concord, does not agree with the way he looked and the way he is at the time. In the first statement it says that Ranko Cesic has brown hair, brown eyes and hair of medium length. You have evidence from the Prosecution, you have the accused here, you have another statement made by a witness who said that he had very short hair, that he had black hair. So this is probably also a reason for which this statement wasn't taken into consideration. With regard to the other witness, on the last page, you also have a description of the accused. It says that Ranko Cesic is very tall, well built, has a big stomach and gaps between the teeth. So the other witness also provided a totally different description of Ranko Cesic, and this is probably the reason for which these statements were never given much weight as evidence. They can't now be taken into consideration as evidence if one is attempting to refute the Defence's arguments that Ranko Cesic's character is good. Our position is that if it is the position that the accused didn't have any prior criminal convictions, this has to be based on evidence, and we have been provided with evidence from the Prosecution. The Prosecution has also provided information from some witness statements according to which the accused had problems with the police. These are rumours. These aren't facts that have been established, and these aren't claims that can be used to refute the Defence's positions. What the Prosecution provided as evidence is a charge that was made in December 1991. It dates to a period before the war, and the accused was not sentenced. In all legal systems, a suspect is considered to be innocent until he is proven guilty. So the fact that certain proceedings were instituted can't be taken as evidence to back up the claim that his character is bad. So if we can't take -- in addition to the fact that we can't take this into consideration, if we have a look at this act, the essence of this incident, you can see that Ranko Cesic comes from an area where the idea of fairness is important. He protected some Muslims by preventing two men from the opposing side from getting into a fight, from participating into a fight. That's what Ranko Cesic did before the war, he didn't allow two adult men to join a fight, and this is something that is supposed to show that his character is bad [as interpreted], and naturally this is not something we can take into consideration because these proceedings were halted. And likewise, you have this in the documents provided by the Prosecution, and it is stated quite unequivocally that the proceedings were suspended because this Muslim person who was involved in a fight couldn't be reached. You have this in documents produced by the Prosecution, and if I have understood this correctly, you still don't have the translation, but you can see there is a letter from the investigating Judge, 13th of December, 1993, and it says that since Amir from Brcko is not accessible to the state organs of the republic, he's not in Brcko, we suggest that the proceedings be suspended. And it also says, from the SJB station, the person we are trying to contact is not accessible and this is why we're suspending the proceedings. It's because the person involved in the fight was not accessible. Everything that I have stated shows clearly that one such incident where it was not even established whether Cesic was guilty or not, and I have explained what the charges consist of, shows that he had no criminal record before the outbreak of the war. As for the second part of the letter submitted by the Prosecution, you will see from the order bearing the date 28th of September, 1995, there is a report from the president of the military court, who says that Ranko Cesic is to serve a sentence, and it says that he has no previous criminal record. This is found in document bearing the number IK139 through 94. This shows that Ranko Cesic had no previous convictions. We now come to a sentence, a single sentence that Cesic had and that referred to a crime which I am deeply convinced my learned friends call the crime of murder quite by accident. When you say the crime of murder, it implies something similar to what the accused has been charged with before this Tribunal. It should, however, be clearly emphasised that this is actually manslaughter, manslaughter of a good friend, a Serb. This was done by accident, and that is the final judgement of the court. So it was not murder. It was manslaughter, and it was a very close friend, a Serb, who was the victim. If we bear in mind that, as the Defence submits, the Chamber should not accept unproved statements bringing into question the good character of the accused and the fact that there was one trial that was suspended and one where he was convicted of manslaughter of a good friend, a close friend, a Serb, then it is clear that, for the purposes of this Tribunal, the accused does not have a prior criminal record and that his crimes amount to the incidents mentioned in the counts of the indictment. It is therefore quite clear that the Prosecution, with the best of intentions, is unable to bring in facts that have not been proved even if only as counter-arguments refuting the arguments of the Defence about the good character of the accused. Just before the war, the accused protected a friend of his, a Muslim, and this is an indisputable mitigating circumstance. It is beyond dispute because ten statements have been submitted by the Defence, one of them from America where the maker of the statement has absolutely no reason not to tell the truth. And this shows that there was no prior discriminatory behaviour by the accused Cesic. Finally, another fact that supports the Defence submission that the accused was of good character and with no prior criminal behaviour is -- and we will now repeat what the -- what camp inmate A said in his statement, that he knew Ranko Cesic well, that he could not believe that a person like him could do something like that, and that he believed it was done under orders from his superiors. What further proof can be needed of the good character of the accused than a statement by the victim of one of his crimes? If this is not considered as evidence, it must at least be considered very probable as testimony to the good character of the accused. I will not repeat again what was said in the sentencing brief, but when you look at the Todorovic case, Todorovic was sentenced for six counts of sexual assault, three of which were identical. There was one count of torture. There are many tortures. And I won't go into all the counts again, but you will see in Todorovic what he, as the chief of police, was charged with in Bosanski Samac. He was charged with persecution and sentenced to ten years. Therefore, 13 years as the minimum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That will be your final sentence then because we're running out of the tape, Mr. Bakrac, and I thought that upon your indication that we could finish before the break. So if you could -- if you could finish, please. So please, if this was your last sentence, please complete it. And if not, try to find your last sentence very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I did apologise in advance. It's very difficult for me to estimate the time. I will need only two or three more minutes. I only wish to draw this comparison in order to draw attention to something I have not come across yet in the jurisprudence but I feel is relevant, and that is that although practice has shown that comparisons are not very useful, they can be useful both for the victims and their families, because let us not allow the seriousness of the pain of one set of victims to be unfavourably compared with the suffering of a second set of victims. We feel that a drastically higher sentence in comparison to some other sentences in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal could also hurt the feelings of the victims' families, because they must be equal in how their pain and suffering is evaluated if some families see that a perpetrator of a crime has been sentenced to far less than another perpetrator. This would be an unfavourable comparison. I would also like to respond to what the Prosecution said about the practice in the former Yugoslavia. Nullum crimen sine lege means that we cannot apply the later standards. I think that this was already adjudicated in Todorovic, and although the Chamber is not bound by the practice in the former Yugoslavia, the maximum sentence would have been 20 years for this accused, and we feel that all the arguments of the Defence are sufficient for the Chamber to determine that 13 years would meet the purpose of the sentencing. I apologise if I have overstepped my time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We will adjourn now until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, before the break I finished, but at the kind suggestion of my learned friends who followed the transcript, which I was not able to do, I only wish to say that the accused has only one prior conviction which the Prosecution submitted. What I said was that he was convicted of manslaughter under Article 31 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia, and we feel that there is a mistake in the transcript as my learned friends indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the mistake, as we understand it, is the way the crime was interpreted to me by our language assistant was "negligent homicide." The term Mr. Bakrac is using continues to be interpreted on the transcript as "manslaughter." That's the difference as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to try to clarify matters, because homicide or murder negligent homicide or manslaughter are terms that could easily create confusion. I do understand, Mr. Bakrac, and I more or less similarly under the Prosecution that the conviction was on the basis that although Mr. Cesic did not intend to kill someone, that he was blamed for being negligent, which negligence caused the death of the other person. Is that a correct understanding? Let me first ask you. Is that a correct understanding of your position, Mr. Bakrac? Yes. I see you're nodding yes, so I take that for a "Da." Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know the exact elements of the crime as contained in Article 38 of the Criminal Code of the Republika Srpska, but we have described the facts as were set forth in some of the documents. It appeared to be a killing that was -- had some elements of self-defence based on a mistaken belief of fact. In some jurisdictions that would be more like a negligent homicide than a manslaughter. But more than that, I can't add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- I don't think that all the underlying documents have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What document you used to base your conclusions upon, and is that a judgement or is that a police report? Whatever is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was from two or three different documents. At page 22, they're numbered with a handwritten number in the lower right-hand corner. Number 22 is translated as being the verdict of the military court in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which had some of the reasoning as well as page 17, which was the appellate decision of the supreme military court which had reasoning. But detailed facts were contained in the documents at pages 12 -- I'm sorry, 11 through 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is that exactly, the document, pages 11 through to 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't tell you exactly because the first two pages are partial pages. They apparently have been not aligned correctly on the copier, and the first two pages, there's half a page or less because it's canted sideways at a 45 degree angle or greater, and so the title page I cannot tell you where it came from. I believe it comes from the military court in Bijeljina, because the page immediately on top of that is from the military court in Bijeljina, and it appears to relate to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the authenticity of these documents in dispute, Mr. Bakrac? I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We are not disputing the authenticity of that document. We only wanted to say what the sentence was for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But there seems to be a slight disagreement on the exact meaning of what Mr. Cesic was convicted for and sentenced for. The Chamber would like to receive the translations of these parts of the document so that it can make its own assessment on whose interpretation of these documents and the conclusions to be drawn from these documents, as far as the conviction is concerned, is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will submit those for translations as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it, Mr. Bakrac, that you have seen those documents, so I take it that -- I take it that you'll receive a copy of the translation as well so that you can at least have tested whether the translations are correct, but apart from that, the authenticity of the documents is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The authenticity of the documents is not in dispute. I trust my learned friends, and I received the document from my learned friends, and this document says what the crime is. And on the front page I have received this judgement which contains the judgement and the legal description of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber expects to receive the translation of all the parts of the document you have just mentioned. That is, what you considered to be the verdict, the decision of the Appellate Court, and the decision pages 11 to 16. That being clarified, I'll just see whether the Bench has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Liu has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions which is firstly addressed to the Defence, Mr. Bakrac. I think in your presentations today, you mentioned that three of the five murders which your client has been found guilty of are kind of momentary incidents. What do you mean by saying that is they are momentary incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I am not in a position to evaluate this and it's not contained in the factual basis. What I was trying to say was that both murders were committed by shooting from firearms, which means there was no additional maltreatment of the victims or suffering which would be the case in -- if another method had been used to murder the victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Another issue is about the incident is that the Prosecution does not agree a word called "isolated incident." What do you mean by saying the "isolated incident"? You mean by the time frame or by the entire environment at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one might say I was referring to the overall situation or, rather, the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The murders were not committed under the umbrella of persecution, of discriminatory intentions or a previously developed system. We feel that these incidents are not connected to each other. They happened during the ten days when the war had just began, when there was a lot of confusion and very strong war propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question is about the paragraph 66 in your recent submissions. You acknowledge that although in this Tribunal's practice there are different views with respect to age and the justification of the age to be taken into account as a mitigating circumstance, at the same time, you also mention that your client, when he was -- when he committed those crimes, was at an age of 27 and a half, and the conclusion you've drawn from this paragraph is that your client's temporary criminis age is another mitigating circumstance. What do you mean by saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that in the jurisprudence, consideration was given to the age of the perpetrator. I can't refer to any particular case right now, but this circumstance was taken as a mitigating factor. However, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has not established a boundary, a limit as to what age can be taken as a mitigating circumstance, so that we feel this can be dealt with on a case-by-case basis. We felt that in view of the circumstances, the age of the perpetrator, the accused, may be considered to be young and can, therefore, be taken as a mitigating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, according to the practice of most of the jurisdictions, the age of adults is 16 or 18 years old, but here you clearly state that your client's age was 27 and a half at that time, so I'm a little bit surprised by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, you are quite right, and according to the legal system of the country that I come from there are minors but also young adults. Such a classification does exist too. I really didn't have time to consult examples, but I just wanted to mention the possibility that this age could also be taken into consideration. In a wartime situation, this might be taken to be a young age which prevents one from acting in a mature way and making decisions as a mature adult, and especially when you find yourself within the context of the vortex of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question is that you mentioned that according to the local law, the maximum punishment is 20 years' imprisonment. Could you please shed more light on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, if I'm not mistaken, in the Todorovic case that was an issue that was discussed. For war crimes, according to the law of the former Yugoslavia, the minimum sentence was five years, and the death penalty, which could also be replaced by a 20-year prison sentence was also provided for. So the maximum penalty in the former Yugoslavia was a 20-year term in prison, which would replace the death penalty. The longest sentence in prison was 15 years. Since the death penalty was abolished in our legal system, and I assume that this is the case in all other legal systems, the main principle is that the most beneficial ought to be applied to the accused if a change has been introduced to the law since the crime was committed. So I think that there is nothing to substitute a 20-year prison sentence, which would be the longest sentence. And the Prosecution, which has claimed that the new law of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1987 should be applied, which provides for a sentence ranging between 20 and 40 years. I don't think this could be applied at all because this would also be contrary to the nullum crimen sine lege principle, which is familiar to all legal systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may ask: Perhaps if you would -- it says the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1987, and that would violate the nullum crimen sine lege. Is that a correct understanding, it's 1987?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. From 1998, because in 1987, Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the law in Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same law as the territory of the former Yugoslavia. When I said that the maximum sentence was 15 years, that was at that time, but the Prosecution in its brief - I don't know exactly where it is, I can have a look for the paragraph - the Prosecution argued -- yes, it's 66. And they mention the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just pointing at a number in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And when I mentioned this principle nullum crimen sine lege, this refers to the law from 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the last question: Do you understand that this Tribunal will not be bound by the local law and the practice as well as the plea agreement reached by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand that, and I have also informed my client of this. He understands this too. In my brief, I didn't refer to the jurisprudence in the former Yugoslavia. This was just a response to part of the Prosecution's brief, the part where they mentioned the practice in the former Yugoslavia, so I thought that it would be appropriate for the Defence counsel to also express its position with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Liu. I have a few questions, and perhaps some of them could be more easily answered by Mr. Cesic himself, but before I address the Defence, first I have a question for the Prosecution. Mr. Hannis, quite some attention has been paid to the consequences of the crimes for the family of the victims, the effect on the victim families. For example, I see that in paragraph 30, you are referring to a statement in which it is said that the mother of Mr. Mujagic suffers from mental disturbance as a result of the killing of her son and how terrible it must be to lose a son. She is at the age of 72, and apart from the statement itself, is there any other source that could -- that could confirm the causal relationship between the mental disturbance and what had happened to her son? And a similar question would be we find in Annex A, we find a relative of one of the victims talking about loss of weight and also about disorder of an immune system which, as I understand, might not be easy to relate directly in a causal relationship with what had happened. Is there any further support for that or what's your view on the evidence needed to -- to establish such causal relationships?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have additional information other than those statements directly from the victims themselves. However, I would indicate that the question was phrased to them when they were interviewed, "Can you tell us how this crime that was committed against you or against your relative has impacted you?" and this was the answer they gave. I understand there could be all sorts of other contributory factors to that ultimate condition as to each of those, but that was what they related their condition to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Now, I would like to ask a few questions. In the sentencing brief it is said that Mr. Cesic is -- well, has an income at a relatively low level, but I don't think it's entirely clear what professional activities of Mr. Cesic have been, well, let's say since the war is over. Could Mr. Cesic or could you inform the Court about the precise development? Was he employed, where, and when?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have confirmation that he was a leather craftsman, that after the war and after he left Brcko, as far as I am aware, he did not have any income.
