He lives with his wife whom he married before he came to The Hague, before he was arrested, and he lived with her before as well. She works as an agricultural technician in a place near Belgrade, and that was the only source of income for him. In addition, I attached to my brief certificates from Brcko which show that he hasn't been taxed as the owner of property of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did he leave Brcko? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to admit that this is something you're going to have to ask Mr. Cesic. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, I do understand that you finally lived in Belgrade. When did you leave Brcko and move to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, towards the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Bakrac, I read on my screen that you said that Mr. Cesic married before he was arrested. I found in the pre-trial brief that he married after the war ended. You -- when exactly was Mr. Cesic arrested? Because we find that in the Prosecution's -- in the Prosecution's sentencing brief, I think it says it was on the -- let me just -- it's in the procedural history. Let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I could clarify this. It is my mistake. I was probably imprecise but it wasn't my intention to be imprecise because these are facts that are not in dispute. When I said after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was speaking in a very broad sense. To be precise, the accused Cesic got married to someone with whom he lived, and this, according to our legal system, was considered to be something like a marriage. It was on the 30th of May, 2002. That's when he officially got married in the premises of the central prison of Belgrade, before he came to The Hague. If I'm not correct, I think the accused will correct my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the documents, I also learned that he was arrested on the 25th of May and that he married officially on the 30th of May. Yes. And that's certainly after the war had ended. I have another question to you in respect of the paragraph 66 you referred to and about the rule nullum crimen sine lege. Would you agree with me that the most favourable law should be applied if the law changes after the crimes have been committed? Is that what you understand as part of the rule nullum crimen sine lege?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understand it, and this is what I stated awhile ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just for sake of argument assume a system in which for a certain crime there is compulsory capital punishment. Yes. So everyone that commits that crime should be sentenced to death. If now the law changes and says the death penalty will not be applied any more, but you get a prison sentence up to 50 years, is it your understanding of the rule of nullum crimen sine lege that he could neither be sentenced to death because that was the heavier punishment, but could he then get the 50 years after that as the more lenient rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a prison sentence is more lenient than the death penalty. That's certain. The problem of applying the law in the former Yugoslavia is one that is perhaps a little more familiar to me. The practice, I don't have the exact information at the moment, though, was such that no crime was subjected to the death penalty as a matter of course. They said that the minimum prison sentence would be 20 years or the death penalty. Since the former Yugoslavia had two republics and it had a federal law, these republics also had their laws and constitutions. The constitution of the federal state abolished the death penalty and the republics retained the death penalty. And at the time that overlaps with the time during which these crimes were committed you had the death penalty on paper but it was never implemented. The 20-year prison sentence would replace it so that problem, that legal problem, still exists because we are still processing certain crimes that were committed far earlier around this time. So this is a constant discussion whether the new law which is in force in Yugoslavia, is it possible for a prison sentence of 40 years to be handed down. Is that a more lenient sentence or is it a more severe sentence than the one that provided for the death penalty? But this has in fact been abolished from the federal constitution, and in its place the 20-year prison sentence would be applied. So I didn't want to enter into this matter above all because I am aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber is not bound by the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia, although it takes this practice into consideration, the Trial Chamber can decide at its discretion. But I just wanted to express my position with regard to what the Prosecution stated, and I am glad, I have to admit, that you asked me about this because I wanted to clarify this issue and have the opportunity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any case law, for example, when the 20 to 40 years was introduced, is there any case law which says that you could not sentence someone to 25 years where the crime was committed under the old regime which still provided for the death penalty because this was the more -- the 20 years was the more lenient system? I'm just asking whether you look at that system as a whole or whether you split it up in several parts and say this is the lenient part of the whole law or you say the whole law in general terms is more lenient than the old one because the capital punishment has been abolished and instead of that we now restrict ourselves to prison sentences, although to a higher limit than before. Should we look at it as a whole or should we look at specific parts of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I've just tried to clarify my position. We're talking about the practice in the former Yugoslavia. I couldn't provide a simple answer to that question. Naturally a term of 40 year sentence in prison is more lenient when compared to the death penalty. That's my position. But I tried to explain why this matter is still being discussed in my country, and with regard to certain specific examples, I can't tell you what these exact examples are, but there is a discussion as to which law is more lenient, and this discussion is still ongoing in my country, in our legal system. This is why I can't provide you with a simple answer to your question. That is the specific situation that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. My next question is about the judgement issued by the military court. Do I understand well that it's not contested, that Mr. Cesic had a weapon when his friend died and that his friend died as a result of a bullet that was fired from that weapon? I'm not saying intentionally fired, but at least that a bullet that came from that weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is correct. And I think that it's necessary to respond as briefly as possible. It is correct, but I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this incident took place at the time of the war when Ranko Cesic and the members of the army were carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then well understand that Mr. Cesic had -- was allowed to carry an arm at that very moment, even under, as I understand from the information, under private circumstances, in a private home?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that you have quite a lot of experience of cases from that period. There is no strict distinction made. After the 22nd of June, 1992, Cesic was no longer a member of the reserve police force. He was a member of the army, and there were really no strict rules as to when one could carry a weapon, when one could not, given that the war was still raging. I believe that these persons had their weapons at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you for answering these questions. Those are my questions. If the parties would like to finish their submissions by making further short comments, I would allow them to do so for, I would say, not more than five to seven minutes, and the parties should then keep to the core of the case and preferably address issues that newly came up or otherwise really restrict themselves in time considerably. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There were a few points raised by Defence counsel that I wanted to address with the Court. One concerned youth as a mitigating factor. I had not addressed that before, but the Prosecution would argue that the age of 27 and a half is not such a young age as should be counted as a mitigating factor in the circumstances of this case. As part of the Defence submission, they included his military book which shows that he served his initial military service in 1983 or 1984, so we would argue that he's well beyond the age of majority and that youth should not be considered a mitigating factor for him. In addition, Defence raised an argument about Mr. Cesic not having any rank and therefore he should not be seen as a person abusing any -- any power or authority he had. I think Your Honour asked a question concerning that before. I would note that in the supplemental pleading which included the redacted statement of victim A from counts 7 and 8, the sexual assault, in his witness statement at page 6 where he's describing the sexual assault, he indicated that Ranko Cesic had ordered him and his brother to begin performing that sexual act on each other, but then he left for 30 or 45 minutes, and before leaving, Mr. Cesic ordered the other soldiers there standing guard not to let the brothers go and to make them continue until Mr. Cesic returned. So in spite of Defence counsel's argument that Mr. Cesic -- in spite of Defence counsel's argument that the witness said he couldn't understand how Mr. Cesic could do anything like this and that he must have been acting on orders from above, it appeared Mr. Cesic was actually giving orders in this case to the soldier below him or at an equal level to make sure that this act continued until he returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one thing? Passing orders in a direction below does not [include] exclude receiving any orders or any instructions received from above. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes. Where the transcript says "does include" I perhaps have not pronounced the words carefully but I think I said "does not exclude receiving any orders..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I understood you to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it appears different in the transcript. In order to avoid whatever confusion, I just note that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one other argument Defence counsel made concerned the sexual assault and humiliating or degrading treatment count in 7 or 8. He argued that the nature of humiliating and degrading treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war actually subsumes the conduct that we have argued should be considered an aggravating factor. I'm partially willing to concede that may be true as to the count where it's a violation of the laws or customs of war, but that would not be true as to the count where it's a crime against humanity, because the degrading treatment, the humiliating nature of that offence is not an element of rape or other forms of sexual assault as those are defined under crimes against humanity. May I consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Bakrac, any further submissions? I would impose the same time limits to you as I did to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you will probably be surprised, but I think any additional comments would be superfluous. I feel I have spoken enough about all these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, if Mr. Cesic would like to add anything to what has been said today, he will have the opportunity to do so. If you want to consult with him, fine, but I just want to let you know that if he wants to add anything, that this is the moment to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Cesic abides by the statement he made and feels there is no need to repeat it. He begs that this not be interpreted as an absence of sincere remorse. He wanted to repeat what he has already said but we feel there is no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then finally I address both parties for the following issue, an evidentiary issue. I know that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is not entirely clear as to evidence on sentencing. Some Chambers take it that Rule 92 bis would be the rule to be applied, whereas others, rather, rely on more -- I would say more flexible system under Rule 101. I didn't hear anything from the parties as far as formalities of evidence are concerned. May I can take it -- may the Chamber conclude that both parties agree that the Chamber could consider whatever is in the submissions and the attachments that have been provided to the Chamber and that formalities, I see that some of the statements, for example, of the Defence have been given in the presence of a notary public, others have not been, but that the parties expect the Chamber to consider whatever is there. I'm not talking about the weight to be given to it. I'm not going to -- I'm not speaking about the test to be applied whether aggravating circumstances should be dealt with in a different way, but just as the source of evidence that we could consider whatever is in the documents submitted to the Chamber. May I? Mr. Bakrac first perhaps for this time. It's always the Prosecution who is first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to say that all the evidence presented by the Defence and attached to the sentencing brief and all the documents submitted by the Prosecution along with their sentencing brief were previously discussed between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence counsel, and I believe that the Chamber was also informed of this. I could have had these statements certified in Bosnia and Herzegovina or with the Registry or we could have called all the witnesses but we felt this evidence would not be challenged and that's why we didn't do this. We also feel that the Prosecution has accepted the documents submitted by the Defence along with the Defence sentencing brief. I felt it necessary to mention this precisely because the Defence does not agree with the evidence submitted after the submission of the sentencing brief, that is, the additional documents that were added on later, for the following reason, Your Honour -- that is I have already stated the reasons in my closing arguments, so I will not repeat them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I have the position of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had had discussions with Mr. Bakrac before -- before today, and we had agreed to a less formal procedure, intending that the Court would accept those documents, because we've had satisfactory dealings in the past and felt comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just wondering about the additional documents that were added on later. There's no agreement upon that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. We did not have any agreement about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be clear that the Court asked for the production of at least some parts of that material, especially since the authenticity is not contested. So certainly to that extent, it will be used. The reason why I'm raising it is because I didn't want any -- any confusion as far as the expectation of the parties is concerned in respect of how we would deal with evidentiary issues and the position of the parties seems to be clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would very much like the Defence to file in detail its objections against the use of the later added documents in writing. So if you would please address that within one week from now on, and of course the Prosecution is invited also to provide the translations of the relevant parts of the documents as soon as possible. Would one week be possible or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with the weight of the Court behind the request, we hope that we can get that in a week, either between CLSS and or our own language assistants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take them perhaps a bit more time. Let's say within 12 days. Then the course the same would be true for -- the same time limit would apply for the submission of the Defence. Yes. Then this -- yes, Mr. Bakrac. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I do apologise. You probably misinterpreted my attempt to see what the last day of the deadline would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this concludes this sentencing hearing in which we heard the submissions of both parties, and we have heard your answers to some questions, Mr. Cesic. The sentencing judgement will be delivered in due course. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: ---  Whereupon the Sentencing Hearing adjourned at
